chapter_theme: The close of the Arkkachandra debate: Neelakesi charges the Buddhist monk with preaching compassion while eating flesh, impermanence while building mansions, and suffering while grumbling over comforts; she refutes his reply that only the mind matters, shows his void release to be no goal at all, teaches him the Jain path of conduct, knowledge and vision, and wins him over, after which he names Mokkalan as his teacher.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist monk (also called சூரிய சோமன்) whom Neelakesi debates and converts

250.reading: Neelakesi asks the monk whether he, wearing the guise taken from one who held that living on in the house of one's birth is a fault, yet full of unworthy things everywhere, can even speak of the high matter of renunciation.
250.nuance: The monk is called by the guise word அவாச்சிய (line 2, after sandhi), which 259 repeats as his title; its sense (perhaps 'one not to be spoken of', perhaps a Buddhist monk's title) cannot be fixed from the verse. Line 3 (சிறந்த வல்லன சிங்கின) is obscure, so the charge of unworthiness is read from the frame of the argument.

claims.claim: the Buddha taught that staying in the household is a fault and one must leave home
one whose life belies the renouncer's guise cannot teach renunciation

251.reading: Neelakesi lists the monks' contradictions: they preach great compassion but eat fish and flesh, spread soft beds yet claim lofty penance, claim to dissolve evil deeds, and what they have found is the void; she asks whether so faulty a path holds together.
251.nuance: The verse is built as a run of paired verbs (உரைப்ப/உண்பன, திரைப்ப/செய்வ), each pair setting a word against a deed. The void (சூனியம்) is named here as the Buddhist goal; the charge that it is empty is answered at length in 262 and 263.

claims.claim: preaching great compassion while eating fish and flesh is self-contradictory
the truth the Buddha saw is the void

252.reading: Neelakesi says they call everything impure, yet bow only at the feet of their own defiled master, call him Sugata though they speak of no bliss, and declare the toil of others' austerities to be worthless.
252.nuance: சுகதன் (Sugata, 'the one gone well') is played against சுகம் (bliss): the title promises the joy the doctrine is said to deny. Lines 2 and 4 do not divide with certainty (அழுக்குற் றவனடிக் கேத்தலர், பல்லார் வருத்தம்), so the reading is tentative.

claims.claim: all things are impure
the hardship of bodily austerity is futile

253.reading: Neelakesi mocks them as people who say all things do not last yet accept goods, raise mansions like mountains, and treat life as a thing with a price: such is the understanding of those who sit in baseness.
253.nuance: The doctrine of impermanence is turned against the monastery: those who teach that nothing stays build as if to stay. Line 2 (மலையோ ரனையந்ன்) and line 3 (விலையே யுயிரென் றிறந்த நினைப) are corrupt or hard to divide.

claims.claim: all things are impermanent
those who teach impermanence while building great dwellings belie their teaching

254.reading: Neelakesi says they cultivate friendliness toward creatures and then sit eating those very creatures' flesh as if devouring them, and knock their heads before a shrine; the ways of madmen are just like this.
254.nuance: மயித்திரம் (maitri) and சயித்தியம் (caitya) are Sanskrit-derived Buddhist terms used precisely, and பயித்தியம் (madness) rhymes on them; the mockery is in the sound as well as the charge.

claims.claim: monks cultivate friendliness toward all beings
one who meditates on friendliness toward beings and then eats their flesh acts like a madman

255.reading: Neelakesi says they set on their heads and worship a copy of a copy of the Buddha's form, and when a creature has died they chew its red flesh: such is the kind of grace their master taught.
255.nuance: செத்த பொழுதின் (when it has died) points at the defence that flesh of an animal not killed for the eater is allowed; the verse only sneers at it, and 260 gives the argument against it. The image worship is mocked as twice removed from its original (போலிக்கும் போலி).

claims.claim: flesh of a creature that has already died may be eaten

256.reading: In a mocking song, Neelakesi has the monk cry 'suffering, suffering' when his lice-ridden robe stinks, when the load is heavy, when he sees a prawn and cannot have it, and conclude that since all his endless tasks are suffering, all is suffering.
256.nuance: The refrain துக்கம் துக்கம் and the close சருவம் துக்கம் parody the Buddhist teaching that all is suffering by reducing it to a greedy monk's petty discomforts; a Buddhist would not accept this as the teaching (compare Manimekalai 30, where suffering is traced to clinging). Line 2 (மானறா நோக்கி மணற்சுமையுந்) is unclear.

claims.claim: all is suffering

257.reading: Neelakesi warns that the lies told under cover, the wages taken, the burnings, the felling of living marutham trees, and the quarrels in anger over meat in the hand will without doubt torment them in the burning hell.
257.nuance: The list joins speech (lies), livelihood (wages), harm to living plants and greed for meat; the killing of trees counts plants as lives, a Jain concern. Line 2 (வையத்தஞ் சுட்டனவும்) is uncertain in its object.

claims.claim: lying, harming living trees and quarrelling over meat lead without doubt to the burning hell

258.reading: Neelakesi tells them that, swelling attachment and multiplying ties while showing themselves free of it and seizing what was left in their keeping, they will take a demon's body or else be dragged, merciless as they are, into the dark hell.
258.nuance: அடைக்கலமே வவ்வுநீர் charges the monks with taking deposits entrusted to them; the punishment is graded, a ghost's birth or, more often, hell. The refrain ஈர்க்குமாலோ closes the song begun at 256.

claims.claim: those who swell attachment while appearing free of it and seize deposits are reborn as ghosts or dragged into hell

259.reading: Hearing her teaching, the monk replies to the lady of fragrant hair that there is nothing but the mind, and that our dark-robed Buddhas would not call all that is called evil conduct evil deed.
259.nuance: The monk's defence of the meat charge is that karma lies in intention alone (சித்தமே அல்லதில்லை). This is the Neelakesi's version of the Buddhist view; Manimekalai 30 lists bodily deeds such as killing and theft among the ten evil deeds, so a Buddhist text itself would not accept that conduct is never evil karma.
259.event: Arkkachandran answers Neelakesi's charges by saying that only the mind matters.

claims.claim: there is nothing but mind
what is called evil conduct is not evil karma when the mind is pure

260.reading: Neelakesi retorts that he wants only to eat and will not cut off fault and entanglement; if he says the mind is good, who can believe it, and when a butcher with a knife cuts off leg and head and stabs, will karma not attach when he eats?
260.nuance: This answers 259 and 255: the eater who did not kill still shares the killing. The phrase இல்லில்வாழ்பேய் (the demon that lives in the house) is read here as a figure for the household butcher, but that is uncertain.

claims.claim: eating flesh that another has killed binds karma to the eater whatever his intention

261.reading: Neelakesi says that if the inner mind and outer conduct agree there may be release, but if one takes flesh the fault comes with it and attachment there, and if the two part, the outward guise is just as false: can he prove otherwise by speaking deceit and growing angry?
261.nuance: பாயிரம் is taken as the outward (Sanskrit bāhya) against உள்ளம், the inward; that reading carries the verse and is not certain. The verse answers 259 by refusing to split intention from deed.

claims.claim: release comes only when the inner mind and outward conduct agree

262.reading: When she tells him that, if on reflection nothing that is stands, the release he dresses up comes to this, that the truth is to become void, the monk, grieving and sighing, asks her, good lady, what he should do.
262.nuance: The verse turns on என்றாட்கு (to her who said): lines 1 to 3 report her reductio, line 4 his surrender. Line 1 (போகவுண் டாக தந்தே) is hard to divide.
262.event: Arkkachandran, unable to answer her, asks Neelakesi what he must do.

claims.claim: on reflection nothing endures

263.reading: Neelakesi says that even if the dead went straight among the gods, people would not look to that joy but would fear death; so we grieve for the Buddha who taught a void release without saying there would be anything to hold to, and she bids the lamenting man leave it.
263.nuance: The argument is from fear: if even death that leads to heaven is dreaded, a release that is only voidness can attract no one. தொத்து (something to cling to) names what the void release lacks. The close (அத்த புலம்பனீ போக) can be read as a dismissal of the Buddha or a bidding to the monk to stop lamenting.

claims.claim: release is a void
a release that is mere void can be no goal, since people fear even a death that leads to heaven

264.reading: The woman further tells him that, fortunate in having cast off all base paths, if he takes up well the good path, good knowledge and right vision and walks by her word, he will reach unfailing great bliss and abide forever.
264.nuance: நன்னெறி, நன்ஞானம், காட்சி are the Jain three jewels (conduct, knowledge, vision), given here as the path that replaces the void release.
264.event: Neelakesi teaches Arkkachandran the path of right conduct, knowledge and vision.

claims.claim: right conduct, right knowledge and right vision lead to lasting, unfailing bliss

265.reading: As a rutting wild elephant from the forest is bound hand and foot, mounted and driven with the goad, so Suriya Soman, first among the Buddha's followers, was bound and taken by the rope of the good lady's words.
265.nuance: சூரிய சோமன் (sun-moon) is a Tamil rendering of the name Arkkachandra (அருக்க, sun; சந்திரன், moon), which 266 gives directly.
265.event: Arkkachandran is won over to the Jain dharma by Neelakesi's speech.

266.reading: Having made Arkkachandra take up the dharma, she bade him say quickly who had taught him these things, and he said it was Mokkalan, the Buddha's chief disciple, who had gone to Murukkuvay.
266.nuance: முருக்குவாய் is taken as a place name; the line could also be read otherwise. The naming of the teacher sends Neelakesi on to the Mokkala debate of the next sarukkam.
266.event: Arkkachandran, now converted, names Mokkalan, the Buddha's chief disciple, as his teacher.

links.note: 259 says only the mind counts and conduct is not evil karma; 261 answers that release needs mind and outward conduct to agree.
links.teaches: The debate's central point is here: the Jain refuses to let a pure intention excuse a deed, so the meat question becomes a question of whether karma lives in the mind or in the act.

links.note: The Neelakesi's monk says evil conduct is not evil karma if the mind is pure; the Manimekalai's Buddhist teacher counts killing, theft and lust of the body among the ten evil deeds that lead to hell.
links.teaches: Set beside a Buddhist epic's own list of bodily evil deeds, the monk's mind-only defence shows itself as the Jain poet's construction of Buddhism, not the doctrine a Tamil Buddhist text teaches.

links.note: 256 parodies 'all is suffering' as a greedy monk's complaints; the Manimekalai teacher gives suffering as the first truth and clinging as its cause.
links.teaches: The parody works by dropping the cause: the Buddhist epic ties suffering to clinging and its end to non-clinging, which the Jain song omits so the doctrine sounds like grumbling.

links.note: Kural 256 argues that no one would sell flesh if no one killed to eat; 260 presses the same point against a Buddhist who says he only eats what another killed.
links.teaches: The Kural's demand argument is put to work against a named defence, the eater's pure intention, and becomes a claim about karma: the buyer's deed joins the butcher's.

gains.a: the retort to the monk gets a general reason why eating implies killing, which the verse only asserts
gains.b: the couplet's abstract buyer is given a real opponent, a monk who claims his mind keeps him clean

links.note: 255 mocks those who eat a creature's flesh once it has died; Kural 258 says those of faultless sight do not eat flesh that has parted from life.
links.teaches: The Kural's phrase 'flesh parted from life' already covers the Buddhist allowance for meat from an animal that died, so the Jain jibe can claim the couplet's authority against that defence.

gains.a: the sneer at eating the dead creature gains a stated principle that even flesh already lifeless is refused
gains.b: the couplet's wording is shown to answer a specific sectarian defence of meat from animals already dead

links.note: Kural 275 says the hidden conduct of those who claim to be free of attachment brings many evils; 258 charges monks who swell attachment while seeming free of it.
links.teaches: The Kural leaves its 'many evils' unnamed; the Neelakesi names them as a ghost's birth or dark hell, turning a moral warning into a doctrine of rebirth.

gains.a: the charge of hypocrisy is anchored in a recognised rule about false renouncers
gains.b: the couplet's vague cry of evils is filled in with the specific rebirths a Jain expects for such conduct

links.note: Kural 280 says neither shaven head nor matted hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; 261 says the outward guise is false unless mind and conduct agree.
links.teaches: Both discount the guise, but for different reasons: the Kural makes conduct the test of renunciation, and the Neelakesi uses that same test against a monk who makes the mind the only test.

gains.a: the argument that the guise means nothing without matching conduct is given an older authority
gains.b: the couplet's dismissal of outward marks is shown not to support a mind-only view, since its test is still what one does

links.note: 263 mocks the Buddha's void release for giving nothing to hold to; Siddhar 1777 bids the seeker cling close to that which became the void.
links.teaches: Whether a void can be a goal one holds is exactly where they part: for the Jain debater the void offers no support, for the Siddhar it is the one thing to grasp.

gains.a: the debater's objection is shown to rest on taking the void as mere absence, which another Tamil tradition denies
gains.b: the Siddhar's call to cling to the void is set against the strongest objection to it, that no one desires an empty release

source_issues: Verse 253, line 2: மலையோ ரனையந்ன் has a stray ந்ன், probably for அனையநன் (மலையோரனைய நன் மாடம்).

Verse 256: the lines are much longer than the surrounding verses and run words together (பெருமுடுகுநாறுமேற், மணற்சுமையுந்தான்பெரிதாற்); the word division appears faulty, and 256-258 are a different metre (a song with refrain) from the verses around them.
Verse 257, line 4 has an extra refrain phrase (அழல்நரகத் துள்ளேயடுப வாலோ), and 258 has five lines; the refrain may have been written out in full by the editor.
Verse 260, line 1: துத்தலே and தோந்தொடர்ப் பாடு are hard to divide (தோம் தொடர்ப்பாடு?).
